intro: Who made your lunch? Who made your shoes? Many people worked to make them. In this unit, you meet the workers and makers.
You will follow bread from a farm to your table. Then your class will hold a market day. You will buy, sell and count money.
By the end, you can tell a producer from a consumer. You can explain what a market is. You can say why prices go up or down.
bigQuestion: How do workers, makers and buyers help each other get what they need?

timeline.t: A farmer plants wheat seeds in a field.
A truck carries the wheat to the mill.
The mill grinds the wheat into flour.
A baker bakes bread, and a store sells it.
Your family buys the bread. You are a consumer.
Room 12 makes bookmarks and cards to sell.
Market day: buyers and sellers meet and trade.
The class counts the money and plans next time.

words.d: a person who makes goods or gives a service
a person who buys or uses goods and services
things people make that you can touch, like bread or shoes
a job one person does to help another, like a haircut
a place where buyers and sellers meet to trade
a person who pays money to get something
a person who gives something in trade for money
how much money you pay to buy something

test.q: A farmer grows corn. What is the farmer?
test.why: The farmer makes a good, so the farmer is a producer.
A shoe is a thing you can touch. That makes it a good.

test.q: You drink milk. What are you?
test.why: You use the milk, so you are a consumer.
A mill grinds wheat into flour.

test.q: Why is a truck driver important for bread?
choices: The driver eats all of it
test.why: Moving goods is transportation. It gets bread to the store.

choices: A place where buyers and sellers meet
test.why: Buyers and sellers meet at a market to trade.

test.q: Nobody buys the paper flowers. What might happen?
test.why: When nothing sells, a seller may lower the price.

test.q: Three bookmarks cost 10 cents each (example). How much for all three?
Everyone wants the cards. What can happen?
test.why: When many buyers want something, it can sell out.

test.q: Which rule makes a market fair?
test.why: Honest signs help buyers trust sellers.

write.prompt: Plan a table for market day. What will you make? What price will you pick (a class example)? What will you do if nobody buys? Draw or tell your plan.
tips: Say what product you will make.
Name the resources you need, like paper and markers.
Write your price on a sign. Keep it honest.
Tell what you will do if it does not sell, or if it sells out.
